newsitem.title: USA: More mishaps hit lower Mississippi River.
newsitem.headline: More mishaps hit lower Mississippi River.

text.p: Swift currents and rough weather played a part in several accidents on the lower Mississippi over the weekend, as raging waters continued to hamper maritime traffic, Coast Guard officials said.
While water levels on the river have been gradually subsiding for more than a week, the improvement offered little relief to ship operators.
In the most serious incident, a bulk carrier, the Flora, collided late Saturday with the chemical tanker Formosa Six two miles south of the mouth of the river in the Gulf of Mexico.

An "undetermined amount" of ethylene dichloride spilled from the Formosa Six as a result of the collison, said Petty Officer Scott Titilah with the Coast Guard's Marine Safety Office in New Orleans, but no injuries were reported.
In addition to heavy rains, waves reached heights of up to 15 feet at the time of the collision, Titilah said.
"Apparently, the weather on scene at the time was fairly rough," he said.

Farther upriver, a tow of some twenty barges broke apart near Baton Rouge on Monday morning, near the site of several previous mishaps, and a breakaway grain barge struck a Swiss freighter at mile 168 between Baton Rouge and New Orleans on Sunday night.
No spills occurred during the barge accidents, officials said, and river traffic was not significantly disrupted.
Both incidents were under investigation, but Coast Guard officials said the fast-moving current was a likely factor.
Water levels have dropped a foot since the flood-swollen river crested last week, but the Coast Guard said it had no plans as yet to scale back extensive safety curbs imposed nearly a month ago.

Those include strict mimimum horsepower requirements for tow boats, and a daytime-only restriction between Baton Rouge and New Orleans on all southbound, deep-draft vessels carrying volatile chemcials and compressed gases.
Petroleum products such as gasoline are not subject to the daytime-only requirement.

In addition, draft restrictions imposed at the mouth of the river at Southwest Pass remain in place, officials said. Vessels exceeding 100,000 tonnes are limited to drafts of 43 feet, while smaller ships are permitted drafts of up to 44 feet.
((-- W Pollack, New York Commodities Desk +1 212 859 1640))
